title: How do we copy an angle without measuring?
description: An angle is copied onto a ray with a ruler and a compass. One arc on the angle, the same arc on the ray, and the length between the two cuts carried across give two triangles with three pairs of equal sides. Keeko's doubt, a new radius at the ray, is tested and struck out.
teaching_notes: One idea: copy three lengths and the angle comes with them. Watch for students who change the first radius when they move to the new ray.

source: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a point X.
video_script.why: The child can bisect angles but has not yet reproduced a given angle somewhere else.
video_script.substitution: An angle is fixed by a triangle. Copy the three sides of the triangle and the angle is copied.
video_script.anchor: An angle at A: copy it onto a ray from X using only a ruler and a compass, and say why the copy is equal.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko opens the compass to a new radius at X. Then XZ is not equal to AB, the triangles have different sides, and the angle at X need not match.
video_script.payoff_line: Angle Y X Z is a copy of angle eigh

final_answer.value: ∠YXZ is a copy of ∠A, because ΔABC ≅ ΔXZY by SSS
final_answer.spoken: angle Y X Z is a copy of angle eigh, because the triangles are congruent by side side side

never_show: the finished copy before step three
maths_rules: An arc with centre A cuts the arms at B and C: AB = AC.
The same radius from X gives a long arc that cuts the ray at Z: XZ = AB, and every point Y on the long arc has XY = AC.
The compass is set to BC; from Z it cuts the long arc at Y: ZY = BC.
Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY by SSS, so angle YXZ = angle CAB.
Slip: a new radius at X breaks XZ = AB, so the triangles no longer have three equal pairs of sides.
video_script.design: One idea: three copied lengths copy the angle. It assumes the compass carries a length. Keeko's doubt is a new radius at the ray. The given angle stays on the left all through.
open_questions: The worklist names the triangles ABC and XYZ; the matching corners are A with X, B with Z and C with Y, so the file writes XZY.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to build an angle at X on the ray, equal to the angle at eigh. Then we say why.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, put the compass point on eigh, and draw an arc across both arms.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Name the cuts B and C. Then eigh B equals eigh C, as both are radii of one arc.

marks.m2: a long arc is drawn from X
marks.m3: it cuts the ray at Z, with X Z and eigh B marked equal

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, keep the same opening, and put the compass point on X.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Draw a long arc that rises above the ray.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>It cuts the ray at Z. Then X Z equals eigh B, because the radius did not change.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: open the compass to BC; from Z cut the long arc at Y; ZY = BC; join X and Y

marks.m1: the compass spans B C on the given angle
marks.m2: from Z it cuts the long arc at Y

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, open the compass to the length B C on the given angle.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Keep that opening, and put the point on Z. Cut the long arc at Y. Then Z Y equals B C.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Join X and Y with the ruler.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: triangles ABC and XZY: AB = XZ, AC = XY, BC = ZY; SSS gives angle YXZ = angle CAB

marks.m1: the triangles eigh B C and X Z Y are shaded in matching colours
marks.m2: the three pairs of equal sides light up
marks.m3: the angles at eigh and X get matching arcs

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, look at triangles eigh B C and X Z Y.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eigh B equals X Z, eigh C equals X Y, and B C equals Z Y. By side side side, they are congruent.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Then angle Y X Z equals angle C eigh B.

beats.on_screen: Answer: angle YXZ is a copy of angle A, because triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY by SSS
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Angle Y X Z is a copy of angle eigh.
